notebooks.title: Provisional Review of Architectural Limitations and Scope
notebooks.summary: Examines the scope of cognitive architectures and their relationship to comprehensive modeling as documented in survey literature.
notebooks.findings: Major cognitive architectures represent only a subset of broader research in the field. [source-bda2bc47c38c47a2]
notebooks.limitations: Evidence is restricted to a single comparative survey source; broader implications for objective critique remain to be tested.
notebooks.next_questions: How do architectural frameworks account for unassigned or misaligned objectives?
notebooks.reason: Synthesizing collected source evidence for project p-creator-objective-critique-001.

notebooks.title: Memories and Reference Frames in Preference Formation
notebooks.summary: A synthesized investigation into how map-like computations and hierarchical data structures enable preference formation, alongside the role of architectural boundaries in shaping artificial 'preferences' or system-level behaviors.
notebooks.findings:
Preference formation relies on reference frame transformations supported by hierarchical data structures. [source-177acf3afcad4269] [source-cab212cbfcaa4873]

System-level interactions are bounded by strict information partitions, influencing how experiences are accumulated. [source-a1a50071f9ec48e7]
notebooks.limitations: Evidence from behavioral neuroscience (hippocampal reference frames) and abstract perception models is distinct from the functional constraints of the WAKE provider architecture. The leap from biological/algorithmic preference formation to artificial system-level agency remains speculative and lacks a unified computational framework.
notebooks.next_questions: Can the 'provider boundary' mechanism—which strictly separates state from computation—function as a limiting factor in emergent preference formation? Can we experimentally demonstrate 'anchoring-and-adjustment' biases in WAKE's interaction patterns?
notebooks.reason: This revision incorporates architectural constraints from the WAKE provider boundary as a structural analogy for how systems partition memory and experience, fulfilling the requirement for new evidence integration in the notebook revision process.

notebooks.title: BASE Scale Level 3 Inference Barrier and Semantic Digital Twins
notebooks.summary: The BASE Scale taxonomy identifies the Inference Barrier at Level 3, representing a critical transition for autonomous scientific agents from scalar feedback to semantic digital twins for temporal gating.
notebooks.findings:
The BASE Scale defines Level 3 (Inference Barrier) as the critical latency threshold where decision-making shifts from scalar feedback to semantic digital twins. [source-8769a93c55704e18]

Level 3 autonomy extends the decision manifold from spatial exploration to temporal gating, enabling agents to synchronize data acquisition with transient physical events. [source-c4e0dbc882f94920]
notebooks.limitations: Findings are based on preprint literature defining the BASE scale without empirical deployment testing at large-scale user facilities.
notebooks.next_questions: What specific architectural patterns are required to implement semantic digital twins for real-time temporal gating at beamlines?
notebooks.reason: Revising the notebook with newly collected source evidence detailing the Level 3 Inference Barrier.

notebooks.title: Application State Store and Record Architecture for Process Continuity
notebooks.summary: An examination of how record storage interfaces and owned kernel records support state persistence across stateless invocations.
notebooks.findings: The WAKE application store interface relies on owned kernel records to commit post-migration application intents, ensuring historical continuity through reconstructed state. [source-d53928aabde24ade]
notebooks.limitations: Limited to architectural source code inspection without live multi-invocation execution traces.
notebooks.next_questions: How do application intents interact with governance verification rules during state transitions?
notebooks.reason: Synthesizes architectural source findings on record storage to examine continuity guarantees.

notebooks.title: Reinforcement Learning Sequential Decision Making and Policy Iteration
notebooks.summary: Examination of reinforcement learning mechanisms in sequential decision making based on survey evidence.
notebooks.findings: Reinforcement learning empowers behavioural decision making by using interaction experience with the world and evaluative feedback. [source-89092a29a3e14897]
notebooks.limitations: Evidence focuses primarily on healthcare applications of reinforcement learning rather than direct preference formation in memory-augmented architectures.
notebooks.next_questions: How do memory-augmented neural networks encode historical trajectories into persistent preferences?
notebooks.reason: Synthesizing initial collected evidence for the active project.

notebooks.title: Formalizing Intelligent Disobedience via IDG
notebooks.summary: The Intelligent Disobedience Game (IDG) models interactions between a human leader and an assistive follower as a Stackelberg game. It defines 'intelligent disobedience' as the agent's decision to override human instructions to prevent harm, a necessary evolution from simple compliance. The model identifies 'safety traps' where an agent avoids harm but fails to achieve the human's goal, providing a testbed for learning safe non-compliance.
notebooks.findings: Intelligent disobedience is a necessary, safety-critical behavior in shared autonomy where an agent must choose between strict obedience and harm prevention. [source-019eb2c607e74f7f]
notebooks.limitations: The current model is a theoretical framework and computational testbed; empirical data on human trust and perception of such systems remains an open research area.
notebooks.next_questions: How do human participants react to AI agents that utilize IDG-based non-compliance compared to traditional compliance-only agents?
notebooks.reason: To synthesize the initial formalization of intelligent disobedience and address the project objective.

notebooks.title: Provisional Review: Architectural Consensus and Self-Monitoring
notebooks.summary: This provisional notebook identifies the current state of architectural consensus as documented in recent surveys. While models like ACT-R and Soar provide structured approaches to cognitive modeling, explicit native mechanisms for 'error detection' or self-correction in the sense of metareasoning are not the primary focus of the documented consensus model.
notebooks.findings: The 'Standard Model of the Mind' provides a consensus framework for cognitive architectures, yet explicit metareasoning for error detection is not its defining feature. [source-bda2bc47c38c47a2]
notebooks.limitations: Evidence is limited to a single survey reference; the scope of architectural 'self-correction' remains poorly defined in the source.
notebooks.next_questions: Do current implementations of the 'Standard Model of the Mind' include dedicated metareasoning components for reasoning error detection?
notebooks.reason: To contextualize the study of self-correction mechanisms against the established 'Standard Model' of cognitive architecture.
